lead: Two bodies meet, push hard for a very short time, and separate. The forces are internal to the pair, so total momentum does not change. A single number, the coefficient of restitution, says how much of the approach speed along the common normal is returned as separation speed. That normal is the line of impact. Direct impact keeps every velocity on that line; oblique impact has sideways velocity too. The same two equations settle both cases. Car bumpers, cricket bat and ball, and train buffers all use this model.
prereq: You need: impulse and momentum from 5.7, and resolving vectors from 5.2.

sections.h3: The line of impact and central impact

blocks.text: A collision lasts a very short time. During that time the push between the bodies is much larger than other forces, so the pair can be treated as isolated. The common normal at the point of contact is the line of impact. It is the only direction in which the collision changes velocity.

Central impact means both centres of mass lie on the line of impact. Then the bodies do not start to spin, and particle theory is enough. Direct central impact means all velocities lie on that line before and after. Oblique central impact means each velocity has a component perpendicular to the line as well.

blocks.where: v₁ and v₂ are velocities along the positive line of impact just before impact; v₁′ and v₂′ are the velocities just after; e is the coefficient of restitution, with 0 ≤ e ≤ 1. Use the same positive direction for all four.

blocks.text: e = 1 is perfectly elastic: separation speed equals approach speed. e = 0 is perfectly plastic: the bodies move together after impact. Real metal, wood and rubber have e between these limits.

sections.h3: Two equations solve a direct impact

blocks.text: For direct central impact write momentum along the line and restitution along the same line. The actual contact force need not be known.

blocks.where: m₁ and m₂ are the masses; v₁ and v₂ are velocities before impact along the line; v₁′ and v₂′ are velocities after impact along the same line.
e is the coefficient of restitution; the right side uses the approach speed along the line.

blocks.text: These are two linear equations in v₁′ and v₂′. Solve them together. If e = 0, both bodies share one final velocity v = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂)/(m₁ + m₂).

items: Choose one positive direction along the line of impact. Put signs on all four velocities.
Substitute masses and signed velocities into the momentum equation.
Substitute e and the approach speed into the restitution equation.
Solve the two equations for the two unknown final velocities.
Find kinetic energy before and after; energy lost = T − T′.

blocks.text: Kinetic energy T = ½m₁v₁² + ½m₂v₂². It always falls when e < 1; the lost mechanical energy becomes heat, sound and permanent deformation.
Resolve each velocity into a component along the line of impact and a component perpendicular to it. Call them v₁n, v₁t, v₂n, v₂t before, and v₁n′, v₁t′, v₂n′, v₂t′ after.

blocks.where: subscript n means the component along the line of impact; momentum is conserved along this line.
subscript t means the component perpendicular to the line of impact; these pass through unchanged when the contact is smooth.
e applies only along the line of impact, never to the perpendicular components.

blocks.text: The perpendicular components pass through unchanged. Restitution is never applied to them. After finding the components, get the final speed of each body from v′ = √(v_n′² + v_t′²). The total kinetic energy uses these full speeds.

For a ball hitting a fixed smooth wall, the wall's mass is effectively infinite. The line of impact is normal to the wall. The normal component reverses with factor e; the tangential component is unchanged. That is why a ball can leave a wall at a different angle from the one at which it arrived.

figure.caption: Before, the 4 kg body at 6 m/s catches the 2 kg body at 3 m/s. Momentum gives the total 30 kg·m/s, and restitution with e = 0.5 gives the separation speed 1.5 m/s, so the final speeds are 4.5 m/s and 6.0 m/s.

spec.title: Direct central impact, e = 0.5

nodes.label: Before
nodes.note: 4 kg at 6 m/s; 2 kg at 3 m/s

spec.aria: Two equations settle a collision: momentum conservation supplies the sum of the final momenta and restitution supplies the difference of the final velocities, giving both answers.

examples.question: Ball A of mass 4 kg moves at 6 m/s and overtakes ball B of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s along the same straight line. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find the velocities just after impact and the final kinetic energy. Take the original direction as positive.
steps: Let v_A′ and v_B′ be the final velocities in the positive direction. Momentum: 4(6) + 2(3) = 30 kg·m/s, so 4v_A′ + 2v_B′ = 30, or 2v_A′ + v_B′ = 15.
Restitution: v_B′ − v_A′ = e(u_A − u_B) = 0.5(6 − 3) = 1.5 m/s. Hence v_B′ = v_A′ + 1.5.
Substitute: 2v_A′ + (v_A′ + 1.5) = 15, so 3v_A′ = 13.5 and v_A′ = 4.5 m/s. Then v_B′ = 6.0 m/s.
Kinetic energy before: ½(4)(6²) + ½(2)(3²) = 72 + 9 = 81 J. After: ½(4)(4.5²) + ½(2)(6²) = 40.5 + 36 = 76.5 J. Loss = 4.5 J, positive because e < 1.
examples.answer: v_A′ = 4.5 m/s and v_B′ = 6.0 m/s in the original direction; final kinetic energy is 76.5 J.

traps: Restitution applies only along the line of impact. In oblique impact the perpendicular components do not change; applying e to them is wrong.
Fix one positive direction along the line and keep signs on all four velocities. Mixing speed and velocity signs makes e come out negative or above 1.
e = 1 means no kinetic energy loss, not that final speeds equal initial speeds. e = 0 means a common final velocity, not zero velocity.
Central impact needs both centres on the line of impact. If the line misses a centre, rotation appears and this particle model is incomplete; see Unit 6.
In oblique impact, momentum is a vector. Conserve it component by component; do not add total momentum magnitudes.

quiz.q: Define coefficient of restitution for direct central impact.
quiz.a: e = (v₂′ − v₁′)/(v₁ − v₂), with velocities positive along the line of impact; 0 ≤ e ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why is total momentum conserved in a collision even though each body's momentum changes?
quiz.a: The contact forces are internal and equal-opposite. The external impulse over the very short impact time is negligible, so total momentum does not change.

quiz.q: Body 1 has mass 2 kg and speed 5 m/s; it catches body 2 of mass 3 kg moving at 1 m/s in the same direction. e = 0.4. Find the final velocities.
quiz.a: p = 2(5) + 3(1) = 13 kg·m/s. Restitution: v₂′ − v₁′ = 0.4(5 − 1) = 1.6 m/s. With v₂′ = v₁′ + 1.6 and 2v₁′ + 3v₂′ = 13, v₁′ = 1.64 m/s and v₂′ = 3.24 m/s.

quiz.q: A smooth wall is hit by a ball at 10 m/s; the velocity makes 30° with the wall normal. e = 0.6. Find the speed after impact.
quiz.a: Normal component before: 10 cos30° = 8.660 m/s. After: −0.6(8.660) = −5.196 m/s. Tangential component stays 10 sin30° = 5.000 m/s. Speed = √(5.196² + 5²) = 7.21 m/s.

quiz.q: Two equal masses have a direct elastic impact, one initially at rest. Show their final velocities.
quiz.a: Momentum gives v₁′ + v₂′ = u. Restitution gives v₂′ − v₁′ = u. Adding and subtracting: v₁′ = 0, v₂′ = u. They exchange velocities.

quiz.q: What happens when e = 0 in a direct impact?
quiz.a: The bodies stick and move with v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂). Kinetic energy loss is maximum for the given masses and speeds.
Both centres of mass lie on the line of impact. The impulse through the centres produces no rotation in the particle model.

beyond: Not for the exam. Car bumpers and crash barriers are tuned so that e is low and the passenger cell absorbs energy over a longer distance. Sports engineers measure e for balls and bats to predict bounce. Impact dampers and granular chains use many tiny collisions to kill vibration. Research goes into contact laws that replace a single e with force-deformation models. Search: coefficient of restitution measurement, Hertz contact, impact damper.
